jar_description: Wide-mouth jar of pressure-canned green beans with a lid that pops up and down when pressed after cooling.
visual_signs: Lid moves up and down when pressed, no vacuum seal. Possible cloudy liquid inside jar.
what_went_wrong: Improper seal due to failure to maintain pressure or improper timing during pressure canning.
explanation_tag_text: This jar did not seal properly because it was not processed at the correct pressure or for the right amount of time. Without a good seal, bacteria can grow and produce dangerous toxins. Always follow tested recipes and maintain proper pressure for low-acid foods.
why: A failed seal on a low-acid food like green beans allows bacteria including Clostridium botulinum to grow, risking botulism.
how_to_prevent: Use an accurate pressure canner with a tested recipe, vent for 10 minutes before pressurizing, maintain pressure consistently, and check seals after 24 hours. Reprocess or refrigerate unsealed jars immediately.
volunteer_talking_points: Low-acid foods like green beans must be heated to 240° F using a pressure canner to destroy botulism spores. A lid that moves means no vacuum seal formed, so dangerous bacteria can survive and multiply.
source_excerpt: Pressure canning produces temperatures high enough (240°F) to kill bacteria including Clostridium botulinum; unsealed jars or improper processing risk botulism

jar_description: A jar of tomatoes canned in a water bath without adding lemon juice or citric acid.
visual_signs: Jar with a bulging lid, cloudy liquid, possibly some bubbles rising in the jar.
what_went_wrong: Low-acid food (tomato) canned without added acid in a boiling water bath, increasing botulism risk.
explanation_tag_text: Tomatoes without added acid are not acidic enough for safe boiling water canning. The bulging lid and cloudy liquid indicate possible bacterial growth and gas formation. Such jars can be unsafe and must be discarded.
why: Without added acid, C. botulinum can grow in tomatoes canned in a water bath, producing deadly toxin. Bulging lids and cloudy liquid signal spoilage.
how_to_prevent: Always add lemon juice or citric acid when canning tomatoes in a water bath. Follow current research-based instructions for acidification.
volunteer_talking_points: Tomatoes are borderline acid foods; adding acid lowers pH to prevent botulism. Bulging lids show internal gas from bacteria, so do not taste or consume.
source_excerpt: Addition of acid in tomato products canned in boiling water bath is recommended; bulging lids or off odors are signs of spoilage and botulism risk

jar_description: Jar of home-canned green chili peppers processed in a boiling water bath instead of pressure canner.
visual_signs: Jar lid sealed but liquid appears cloudy, possible floating pieces, and soft texture.
what_went_wrong: Processing low-acid foods like peppers in a boiling water bath rather than a pressure canner.
explanation_tag_text: Low-acid foods must be pressure canned to reach safe temperatures and kill botulism spores. Boiling water bath doesn’t get hot enough to ensure safety even if the lid seals.
why: Boiling water bath processing does not reach temperatures needed to kill botulism spores in low-acid vegetables. Seal alone does not guarantee safety.
how_to_prevent: Use a pressure canner for all low-acid foods like vegetables and peppers. Follow tested recipes and correct times.
volunteer_talking_points: Low-acid foods can grow deadly botulinum bacteria unless heated to 240 degrees with pressure canning. Don't rely on sealing to mean safe.
source_excerpt: Boiling water canners do not produce temperatures high enough to kill botulism-causing bacteria in low-acid foods; must use pressure canning

jar_description: Jar of jam with white crystals forming on surface and around the edges inside.
visual_signs: Visible white crystallization on surface and near the lid seal inside jar.
what_went_wrong: High sugar content and/or improper sugar ratios causing crystallization in jam.
explanation_tag_text: Crystals are sugar precipitates and not harmful but indicate texture or recipe problems. Jam is safe but may have altered texture. Use precise recipes and sugar amounts to avoid.
why: Sugar crystallization is a quality issue, not a safety concern, as no harmful bacteria grow in high sugar jams.
how_to_prevent: Use tested recipes, dissolve sugar fully, and stir to prevent crystals when cooking jams.
volunteer_talking_points: Crystallization is common from excess sugar or cooling. It doesn’t mean the jam is spoiled but may affect mouthfeel.
source_excerpt: Crystallization occurs because of excess sugar; it’s a texture problem rather than a safety issue【troubleshooting_canned_fruit_spreads】

jar_description: Jar of home-canned carrots with evident mold growing on top of food inside jar.
visual_signs: White cottony mold on surface inside jar and under the lid, possible off-odor when opened.
what_went_wrong: Spoilage due to incomplete processing or seal failure leading to mold growth.
explanation_tag_text: Mold growth inside canned food is a clear sign of spoilage. Do not taste or consume as spoilage organisms may produce harmful toxins.
why: Mold contaminates food making it unsafe to eat. Mold toxins or bacterial toxins like botulinum could be present.
how_to_prevent: Use proper processing times with pressure canning for low-acid foods, ensure lids seal properly, and check jars before storage.
volunteer_talking_points: Any mold visible inside a sealed jar means the food is spoiled. When in doubt, throw it out. Botulism toxin cannot be seen but mold presence means conditions were unsafe.
source_excerpt: Look for mold growth on surfaces or under lids; never taste canned food with mold or off-odors; discard carefully to avoid illness

jar_description: Jar of low-acid vegetable pickles with liquid level far below 1/2 inch headspace.
visual_signs: Liquid in jar does not fully cover vegetables; food exposed to air inside jar, with possible air bubbles rising.
what_went_wrong: Improper headspace causing insufficient liquid coverage and potential spoilage.
explanation_tag_text: Headspace affects vacuum formation and food safety. Not enough liquid to cover food can lead to air pockets, spoilage, or improper sealing.
why: Food not submerged in liquid can spoil or grow bacteria, risking food safety.
how_to_prevent: Follow recommended headspace for product (usually 1/2 inch for acid foods) and ensure food is covered by liquid before processing.
volunteer_talking_points: Correct headspace prevents spoilage and ensures vacuum seals. Too much air can lead to bacteria growth and seal failure.
source_excerpt: Leave ½ inch headspace for fruit and liquid; keep jars upright and submerged during processing to prevent spoilage

jar_description: Jar of home-canned seafood with a leaking lid and liquid slime visible inside.
visual_signs: Leaking jar, sticky or slimy liquid, foul odor upon opening.
what_went_wrong: Leakage due to improper seal or damaged lid allowing contamination and spoilage.
explanation_tag_text: Leaking jars do not have proper vacuum seal and allow bacterial entry. Spoiled seafood can be highly dangerous, discard immediately.
why: Leaking jars are unsafe due to risk of spoiling and botulinum toxin formation in seafood, a low-acid food.
how_to_prevent: Use new lids, clean jar rims, follow pressure canning guidelines, do not reuse damaged lids, and check seals after processing.
volunteer_talking_points: Seafood must be processed in pressure canners and keep perfect seals. Leakage means contamination and unsafe food.
source_excerpt: Unsealed, leaking or open jars should be detoxified before disposal. Leaking jars indicate spoilage and risk botulinum toxin

jar_description: Jar of home-canned mushrooms processed in a water bath canner instead of pressure canner.
visual_signs: Sealed jar with natural color but cloudy liquid, no visible signs of spoilage.
what_went_wrong: Mushrooms, a low-acid food, were water bath canned instead of pressure canned, risking botulism toxin.
explanation_tag_text: Low-acid foods like mushrooms require pressure canning to ensure safety. Water bath canning does not kill all bacteria that produce toxins.
why: Even if jar looks normal, botulinum toxin could be present. These foods must be canned using pressure canning.
how_to_prevent: Always pressure can low-acid foods like mushrooms. Follow tested USDA recipes and times.
volunteer_talking_points: Appearance can be deceiving; botulism toxin has no odor or visual signs but can be fatal. Proper pressure canning is vital.
source_excerpt: Low-acid foods processed improperly in boiling water bath can harbor botulinum toxin even if appearing normal

jar_description: Jar of home-canned salsa with floating vegetable pieces at the top of the liquid.
visual_signs: Vegetable pieces floating near the surface of the jar, liquid below them.
what_went_wrong: Floating pieces due to insufficient pack or poor headspace adjustment causing food to rise during processing.
explanation_tag_text: Floating fruit or vegetable pieces can indicate improper packing or headspace. It affects quality but not necessarily safety if processing was done correctly.
why: Floating pieces usually impact texture and appearance but do not cause spoilage if processing and seal are correct.
how_to_prevent: Pack jars according to recipe instructions, allow correct headspace, and remove air bubbles before processing.
volunteer_talking_points: Floating food is common with some recipes and usually safe but check jars for proper seal and processing times.
source_excerpt: Floating fruit or vegetables can occur from improper packing or air bubbles but is not a safety concern if canning is done properly【troubleshooting_canning_acid_foods】

jar_description: Jar of home-canned pears with lid seal failure; lid easily lifts when pressed and liquid is leaking.
visual_signs: Loose lid that lifts when pressed, liquid stains on jar side from leakage.
what_went_wrong: Seal failure caused by retightening lid after processing or dirty jar rim.
explanation_tag_text: Retightening lids after processing or residue on jar rims can cause poor seals, leading to spoilage and risk of unsafe food.
why: A failed seal lets bacteria and mold enter, spoiling food and causing health hazards.
how_to_prevent: Do not retighten lids after processing. Clean jar rims well before filling and check seal after cooling.
volunteer_talking_points: Retightening hot lids can damage gasket and break the vacuum. Proper jar cleaning and handling help ensure good seals.
source_excerpt: Do not retighten screw bands after processing; retightening hot lids may cause seal failure and spoilage

jar_description: Jar of raw-pack canned plums in water, with floating fruit visible inside.
visual_signs: Fruit pieces are floating near the top inside the jar instead of being evenly distributed or settled.
what_went_wrong: Raw pack plums were canned without proper hot pack step, causing floating fruit.
explanation_tag_text: Floating fruit often happens when fruit is packed raw instead of hot. Raw fruit contains air in its cells that escapes and causes pieces to float during processing.
why: Floating fruit is a quality issue, not a safety risk if proper processing time was followed.
how_to_prevent: Use hot pack method by cooking fruit briefly before packing; this reduces air and prevents floating.
volunteer_talking_points: Raw packing plums leaves air in fruit that rises during processing, causing floating pieces. Hot packing removes this air and helps fruit sink and stay covered with liquid.
source_excerpt: Raw pack plums usually result in floating fruit.

jar_description: Jar of canned cherries with darkened, dull color compared to fresh fruit color.
visual_signs: Fruit inside jar looks darker or brownish; color is not bright or fresh looking as expected.
what_went_wrong: Fruit was either overcooked during preparation or processed for too long causing color change.
explanation_tag_text: Exposure to heat or prolonged processing can cause fruit to lose its bright color and become darker or dull.
why: Color changes affect appearance and quality but do not indicate unsafe food if processing was adequate.
how_to_prevent: Use recommended processing times and avoid overcooking fruit before packing.
volunteer_talking_points: Heat causes natural pigments to break down, changing color. High temperatures or long cooking times degrade quality but not safety.
source_excerpt: Exposure to heat...will decrease quality and shelf life of canned food.

jar_description: Jar of home canned strawberry jam with white, gritty crystals on surface and inside the jam.
visual_signs: Visible white or translucent crystals scattered throughout the jam.
what_went_wrong: Crystallization formed due to too much sugar or improper sugar ratios in the jam recipe.
explanation_tag_text: Excess sugar or incorrect sugar balance causes sugar crystals to form in jams. These crystals affect texture but do not mean the jam is spoiled.
why: Crystallization is a quality defect only, not a safety hazard.
how_to_prevent: Follow tested recipes exactly including sugar amounts and avoid doubling recipes mid-way.
volunteer_talking_points: Crystals form when sugar isn’t fully dissolved or is present in excess. It’s a textural change, not microbial spoilage.
source_excerpt: High sugar content and/or improper sugar ratios causing crystallization in jam.

jar_description: Jar of pickles with cloudy brine inside, green cucumbers visible.
visual_signs: Liquid brine in jar looks cloudy instead of clear; cucumbers appear normal.
what_went_wrong: Cloudy brine formed due to natural fermentation, equipment residue, or non-heat treated pickles.
explanation_tag_text: Cloudy brine can result from natural fermentation or minerals from ingredients. It's usually safe if no off odors or spoilage signs are present.
why: Cloudiness from fermentation or minerals is a quality issue unless accompanied by spoilage signs.
how_to_prevent: Use clean jars, hot pack, and follow recipe recommendations for processing and brine ingredients.
volunteer_talking_points: Cloudy brine often means some fermentation activity, which can affect taste but generally is safe for properly processed pickles.
source_document: UC Davis Common issues with fermented fruits and vegetables
source_excerpt: Cloudiness is common in fermented vegetable products and usually not a safety concern.

jar_description: Jar of home canned fruit pie filling with liquid level noticeably lower than when packed.
visual_signs: Liquid covering fruit is low or missing, possibly fruit is exposed to air inside the jar.
what_went_wrong: Siphoning occurred during cooling due to removing jars too quickly from the canner or insufficient headspace.
explanation_tag_text: Siphoning causes juice or liquid loss from jars due to rapid temperature/pressure change. It reduces quality but is usually safe if sealed.
why: Siphoning is a quality problem, not a safety issue if seal is intact and processing was adequate.
how_to_prevent: Wait 5–10 minutes after processing before removing jars; leave adequate headspace; avoid rapid cooling.
volunteer_talking_points: Hot liquid and air contract while cooling, causing liquid to suck out if jars are moved too soon or headspace is too low.
source_document: PNW 736 Fruit pie filling home canning
source_excerpt: To minimize oozing, turn off heat and wait 5 minutes before removing jars.

jar_description: Jar of canned peaches with fruit floating unevenly near the surface and liquid below.
visual_signs: Some peach slices float at the top leaving gaps below, creating uneven liquid coverage.
what_went_wrong: Insufficient pack density or improper air removal caused fruit to float during processing.
explanation_tag_text: Packing fruit loosely or failing to remove trapped air causes floating fruit pieces during canning.
why: Floating fruit is a visual and quality issue, not a safety problem.
how_to_prevent: Pack fruit firmly and remove air bubbles with a utensil before sealing.
volunteer_talking_points: Air trapped between fruit pieces expands during processing making fruit rise. A firmer pack and bubble release help keep fruit down.
source_excerpt: Raw pack plums usually result in floating fruit.

jar_description: Jam jar with thick jam showing slightly liquid watery layer separating on top after storage.
visual_signs: Liquid or syrup separates and pools on top of jam, leaving a watery layer above thicker gel.
what_went_wrong: Jam did not fully gel due to undercooking or insufficient pectin causing liquid separation.
explanation_tag_text: Liquid separation in jams occurs when there is not enough pectin or cooking time was too short to form a stable gel.
why: This is a texture and quality problem, not a food safety hazard.
how_to_prevent: Follow tested recipes and pectin instructions carefully; cook jam to proper gel point.
volunteer_talking_points: Gel forms from pectin and sugar heating; not reaching the gel point causes weeping liquid but is not unsafe.
source_excerpt: Follow directions exactly; jams should stand to allow gel formation.

jar_description: Jar of canned green beans with noticeably low liquid filling, some beans are exposed above liquid.
visual_signs: Liquid level inside jar is low, not covering food as expected after processing.
what_went_wrong: Improper headspace or liquid loss due to siphoning caused insufficient liquid coverage.
explanation_tag_text: Liquid siphoning or wrong headspace means food is not fully covered, which can reduce quality and cause discoloration but is safe if sealed.
why: Low liquid is a quality issue but not a safety risk if jar sealed and processed correctly.
how_to_prevent: Leave correct headspace and wait recommended time before removing jars from canner.
volunteer_talking_points: Post-processing liquid loss can make food dry or discolored but sealed jars remain safe to eat.
source_excerpt: Avoid siphoning by following headspace and wait-time recommendations.
